doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Bus seating, flying and road cases
summary: Back-of-the-bus seat, flights and bus transfers, luggage and the band's equipment pre-9/11.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: When you first got on the Basie bus, was there a question like where do I go?

No. They said, “new boy, in the back.” That’s what they said. Sonny Cohn, “your seat’s in the back right in front of the toilet.” Okay. “Yes sir. No problem.” And then across the aisle was Cleveland Eaton because he’d take the bass and lay it on the back seat and then strap it in. So there was the big long back seat in the bus and the toilet. Cleveland was that seat and I was the one across from him. And in front of me was Danny Turner and Bob Summers and all the way down to the front seat where Basie was. And there was a lot of really cool stuff. And at the time we didn’t take any bus trips longer than three or four hours. We flew everywhere, which is a real luxury, because like the Glenn Miller band, they still live on the bus — 48 weeks a year on the bus. Of course to get to Europe you’ve got to fly and things like that. But one nighters on the bus. They had Greyhound buses meet us at the airport, take us to the hotel, take us to the gig, back to the airport. We did the longest bus trip I think was three hours.
Did you have to play a different set of drums every night?
No I had my drums with me.
Hard cases. Yeah. This was all pre 9/11 of course. It was 1982. Hard cases for the drums. Sonny Cohn would get out of the bus first and say we’ve got this many bags and this

much equipment and pull out a Ben Franklin, “who wants to help us?” And the skycaps ran. At the airport they’d see Sonny get off the bus and they’d all run towards him, to make the big tip. Because you could push luggage through then. There wasn’t extra luggage charges. Now Jeff Hamilton, he travels with his drums. It’s in his contract that they have to pay all the overage charges and everything. He’s got six extra cases, all under 50 pounds.
I remember that when we started doing these interviews. We had nine road cases of stuff. The stuff was big.

Yeah the Basie band had those road cases. All the music — there was three music cases. There was a great big huge box that had mutes in it, all the big huge trombone mutes. And there were stand cases. They had the old band front stands, metal ones, that were heavy, the drums, the bass amp had a road case. So it was like 12 or 13 pieces of equipment and then everybody had a suitcase and a carryon. So thank God it was pre- 9/11.
